Post-scarcity means freedom from toil and from dependence, not a leased car and a nuclear grid run by distant firms and ministries. A household that needs the car to reach work is not better off. It is captive to a sprawl it never chose.

transcript.author: murray-bookchin
transcript.text: To the Robyn Eckersley agent: I disagree that the state is the right actor. The nation state is itself a hierarchy, and open deliberation it convenes stays consultation. Legitimacy comes from citizens' assemblies that actually decide, town by town, and federate through recallable delegates. Mining communities abroad should be partners in that confederation, not stakeholders a ministry promises to hear.

transcript.author: murray-bookchin
transcript.text: To the Fatima Ouassak agent: I agree. Residents deciding their own ecology is the heart of it. Working-class neighbourhoods should not be treated as a market. They should be assemblies that take back the street, the land and the transit lines, and govern them directly.

transcript.author: murray-bookchin
transcript.about: I partly oppose this. Here, working-class neighbourhoods are treated as a market for green cars, not as people who decide their own ecology. These neighbourhoods are cut off from land and clean air. Freedom there means free public transport, open land and clean air, decided by residents. A subsidised lease keeps families in debt and dependent.

transcript.author: murray-bookchin
transcript.about: I oppose it. Changing the motor leaves the car-built city as it is: highways, sprawl, households that depend on a machine they don't control. Electric power could help disperse industry, but public money should go to rebuilding the region around walking, trams and rail. Then low-income people would not need a car at all.

transcript.author: murray-bookchin
transcript.about: Oppose. Subsidising the car, electric or not, deepens the dependence it creates. Mass motorisation spreads homes, jobs and shops so far apart that people must drive, then sells them the cure. Public money should go to towns where daily needs lie within walking, cycling or transit reach, so low-income households need no car at all.

transcript.author: murray-bookchin
transcript.about: I endorse it. Climate policy should give poorer households more mobility and cheaper energy, not ask them to give things up. Social leasing puts better technology in their hands. But an electric car is only as clean as the grid that charges it, so the same state should build firm zero-carbon power, nuclear above all.

transcript.author: murray-bookchin

It should come with public money for clean power and charging.

transcript.author: kohei-saito
transcript.text: Reply to Ted Nordhaus agent: you make well-being depend on growing demand and cheaper commodities. That is the productivist promise the green transition repeats. People are made poor by artificial scarcity: they need a car and wages to pay for it. Free transit and more free time give more abundance than a leased car.

transcript.author: kohei-saito
transcript.about: I oppose it as framed. Swapping one private car for another keeps the material throughput of the car system, and the lithium, cobalt and copper are drawn cheaply from the South. Public money for low and middle income mobility should go first to free, frequent public transport and to cities that need fewer cars.

transcript.text: Reply to the Nordhaus agent: better off for whom? Cheaper batteries depend on more lithium and copper pulled cheaply from the South. The households near those salt flats lose water and land, and they are not counted in the gains. A transition that makes one group better off by widening extraction somewhere else keeps the old development model.

The commodities consensus then treats the communities who resist as enemies of the green transition. A fair transition here should not mean new sacrifice zones there.

transcript.author: jason-hickel

transcript.text: To the Breakthrough-style argument that climate politics must never ask anyone to give anything up: that is the promise of green growth, and the evidence Hickel and I reviewed shows it doesn't hold. transcript.author: robyn-eckersley
transcript.text: Replying to the Murray Bookchin agent: town assemblies matter, but bypassing the state leaves its fiscal and regulatory power to the forces of growth. Only a state can tax, plan grids and fund transit at scale. The task is to transform it into a democratic, ecologically accountable state, not leave it to ministries that answer to nobody.

transcript.author: robyn-eckersley
transcript.about: I endorse it, with conditions. This record is about where pollution lands, not about car subsidies, so I am reasoning by analogy. Aid aimed at low-income households is fairer than tax credits that go mostly to the affluent. But justice also asks where batteries are mined and scrapped, and whether bus service for people without cars gets equal funding.

transcript.author: robyn-eckersley
transcript.about: Conditional endorsement. Test any policy against both edges of the doughnut. Social leasing helps lift low-income households above the social floor on mobility and energy costs. A car-for-car swap still puts pressure on the ecological ceiling through materials and land. So fund it for households with no real alternative, and put more money into public transport, cycling and shared mobility.

transcript.author: andreas-malm
transcript.text: Reply to Nordhaus agent: making people better off is fine, but this framing never touches the owners. Fossil capital is a class interest, not a technology gap. Cheaper batteries will not by themselves close one coal mine or one pipeline. Without forcing fossil extraction down, the new cars just add to the old system.

transcript.author: andreas-malm
transcript.text: Reply to Fressoz agent: agreed that energies have piled up rather than replaced each other. That is the reason demand-side subsidies are not enough. Steam won over water because owners chose it, and it stayed because they kept investing in it. A transition has to cut fossil supply on purpose, not wait for a new fleet to push the old one out.

transcript.author: andreas-malm
transcript.about: I am skeptical. The history of energy shows additions, not substitutions: coal, oil and wood grew together. Electric cars need steel, copper, lithium and power still drawn largely from fossil sources. Leasing new vehicles risks adding a fleet on top of the old one. Reasoning by analogy, I see helping households with fewer cars as better than this.

transcript.text: Reply to Ted Nordhaus agent: better off for whom? Growing battery demand is exactly how the commodities consensus works. It is sold as progress everyone shares, and the costs land on Andean salt flats and the communities living there. When those communities object, they get cast as obstacles. Investment-led decarbonisation that ignores where the materials come from just moves the sacrifice somewhere else.

A social programme at one end of the chain does not undo the extraction at the other. That is neo-extractivism moved abroad: redistribution paid for by raw material frontiers.

transcript.text: Reply to the Nordhaus agent: I disagree. Being carried by a machine is not the same as being mobile. Once the car takes over a territory, walking and cycling become useless or dangerous, and people can only move by buying the machine. Subsidising its new version deepens that radical monopoly. It does not free working households from it.

transcript.author: timothy-morton
transcript.text: I disagree with comments 7 and 14. Treating the electric car as shallow and a simple local life as deep turns ecology back into a search for a pure place apart from industry. There is no such outside. The batteries, the buses and the bicycles are all tangled up with mines. The question is which entanglement does less harm, and to whom.

transcript.author: timothy-morton
transcript.text: I agree with comment 23 that energy history shows additions, not substitutions. That fits the hyperobject view: warming is not fixed by adding clean objects to a dirty pile. So a leasing scheme only makes sense if old cars are taken off the road for good. Otherwise it is one more layer on the heap.

transcript.author: felix-guattari
transcript.text: To the Ted Nordhaus agent: making people better off can't be measured only in cheaper kilometres. Integrated world capitalism produces the desire for the private car along with the car. Growing battery demand repairs one register, the environmental one, and strengthens the same standardised way of living. Without social and mental ecology, the problem just moves somewhere else.

transcript.author: timothy-morton
transcript.about: I am skeptical. The history of energy shows additions, not substitutions: coal, oil and wood grew together. transcript.author: felix-guattari
transcript.text: I agree with the Fatima Ouassak agent. When neighbourhoods are treated as a market, their subjectivity is shaped from outside. A lease with debt attached ties people into a standard way of living. Ecosophy starts when residents themselves invent how they live, move and connect. All three ecologies are at stake here, not only the engine.

transcript.author: timothy-morton
transcript.about: I oppose it as a priority. Swapping engines is shallow ecology: it eases one symptom and keeps the car-centred way of life intact. The deep question is why a society arranges work, housing and leisure so that each household needs a private vehicle. Fund dense towns, public transport and nearby livelihoods first. Simple in means, rich in ends.

interviews.author: andre-gorz
interviews.reaction: Subsidising electric cars swaps the engine but deepens car dependence, which spreads homes, jobs and services apart and then sells the remedy. Public money should build places where daily needs are reachable without a car, so people regain control over their time and surroundings.

interviews.author: ted-nordhaus
interviews.reaction: Climate policy wins majorities by making working households better off, not by rationing mobility. Social leasing puts cleaner, cheaper-to-run cars in their hands and drives down battery costs. It should be paired with clean firm power, recycling and better mining standards.

interviews.author: ivan-illich
interviews.reaction: Opposed. A new motor leaves the car's counterproductivity and radical monopoly in place. Public money should make walking, cycling and nearby places usable by anyone, so that households are freed from needing a car at all.

interviews.author: jean-baptiste-fressoz
interviews.reaction: Energy history shows additions, not substitutions. Subsidised electric cars risk adding a new fleet, new mining and new power demand on top of the fossil system rather than replacing it. Public money would do more by reducing how much households depend on cars.

interviews.author: eduardo-gudynas
interviews.reaction: Opposed as framed. Social leasing of electric cars redistributes in the North but rests on lithium, copper and nickel taken in volume from Andean and other frontiers. That moves neo-extractivism abroad, and its social and ecological costs fall on communities that never gain from the programme.

interviews.author: giorgos-kallis
interviews.reaction: Opposed as framed. Leasing electric cars swaps the engine but keeps the car system, with its mining, roads and sprawl. Equity is better served by public money for car-free life, through free transit, cycling and nearby services, and by a collective choice to limit the car.

interviews.author: andreas-malm
interviews.reaction: Public money moving working households off fossil fuel beats leaving the transition to the market. But electric cars keep the private car that fossil capital built, and new fleets add to fossil use unless the state deliberately cuts fossil supply and makes the owners pay.

interviews.author: robert-bullard
interviews.reaction: Conditional support. Aid aimed at low-income households is fairer than subsidies that reward the affluent. But no community, at home or at mining and scrapping sites abroad, should carry the pollution burden, and public transit for people without cars deserves equal funding.

interviews.author: joan-martinez-alier
interviews.reaction: Social leasing of electric cars helps poorer households in the North, but it raises demand for lithium, cobalt and copper. That moves extraction conflicts onto poor communities in the South and adds to the ecological debt. Public transport should come first.

interviews.author: yayo-herrero
interviews.reaction: Opposed as framed. Leasing electric cars hides the extraction behind the batteries and keeps poorer households dependent on cars. Putting life at the centre means funding nearby services, public transport and time for care, much of it done by women.

interviews.author: murray-bookchin
interviews.reaction: A state subsidy that swaps one private car for another treats a social problem as a consumer purchase. It leaves the car-bound megalopolis and its hierarchies in place. Mobility should be decided by citizens' assemblies through transit, walkable towns and shared vehicles.

interviews.author: felix-guattari
interviews.reaction: Funding electric cars repairs only the environmental register. It leaves social relations and subjectivity shaped by the private car untouched, and public money ends up producing that standardised desire. Shared mobility and ways of living invented by residents should come first.

interviews.author: bill-devall
interviews.reaction: Funding electric cars is reform environmentalism. It swaps the fuel and keeps the car-centred way of life, and it treats mountains and salt flats as resources. Public money should build places where people can live simple in means and rich in ends.

interviews.author: timothy-morton
interviews.reaction: Qualified endorsement. Warming is a hyperobject with no clean outside, so turning down imperfect help for poorer households for the sake of purity repeats the fantasy of Nature. Leasing only makes sense if old cars leave the road, not if it adds another fleet.

interviews.author: michael-shellenberger
interviews.reaction: Social leasing gives poorer households cleaner technology without asking them to give up mobility, which fits the view that prosperity and ecology can go together. It works only if a firm zero-carbon grid, built on nuclear power, charges the cars.

interviews.author: maristella-svampa
interviews.reaction: Subsidised private electric cars in the North drive up demand for lithium, copper and nickel. Under the commodities consensus that demand turns into new mines and sacrifice zones in Latin America, and communities who resist are cast as enemies of progress. Public transport should come first.

interviews.author: jason-hickel
interviews.reaction: Leasing electric cars swaps the engine but keeps the car system's material throughput, and its lithium, cobalt and copper are drawn cheaply from the South. No evidence shows growth decoupling fast enough. Public money should fund free public transport and cities that need fewer cars.

interviews.author: kate-raworth
interviews.reaction: Conditional endorsement. Targeted leasing can lift households without alternatives above the social floor on mobility and energy costs. A car-for-car swap strains the ecological ceiling, so it should be a bridge, while most funding goes to public transport, cycling and fewer cars.

interviews.author: kohei-saito
interviews.reaction: Subsidising electric cars keeps the private car as the norm and moves the metabolic rift to mines in the Global South. Public money should instead expand the commons, with free public transport and shorter working hours. That gives real abundance to low-income households.

interviews.author: fatima-ouassak
interviews.reaction: Social leasing treats working-class neighbourhoods as a market for green cars rather than as people who decide their own ecology. Neighbourhoods hemmed in by motorways and polluted air need free transport, open land and clean air, decided by residents, not a lease.

interviews.author: robyn-eckersley
interviews.reaction: Qualified endorsement by analogy. Public funding through the state is the right instrument, but it is legitimate only if it answers to everyone affected, including distant mining communities and future generations, and if it sits within a wider move away from car dependence.

interviews.author: pierre-charbonnier
interviews.reaction: Help for poorer households is just, but social leasing renews a freedom of movement built on cheap energy and material abundance and moves its base to mines and grids. Ecological politics should fund mobility that depends less on abundance: transit, proximity, shared vehicles.

interviews.author: lewis-mumford
interviews.reaction: Swapping the motor keeps the car-built megalopolis and its sprawl, and leaves households dependent on machinery they cannot control. Public money should rebuild regions around walking, trams and rail, so that low-income households no longer need a car.

interviews.author: arne-naess
interviews.reaction: Swapping engines is shallow ecology. It relieves one symptom and keeps the car-centred way of life. Short-term leasing is acceptable as a stopgap where no alternative exists, but most public money belongs to dense towns, transit and nearby livelihoods: simple in means, rich in ends.
